institutionName: Panteion University of Social and Political Sciences

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: For me, it was important to choose a destination that was somewhat foreign to me, so that I could spend my time exploring a new culture while being on exchange. It was also important that the academic classes i could follow gave me new perspectives on my study program, than i could have had back home. Lastly I wanted to choose a destination which I new would be accomodating to exchange students, and where there would be a lot of opportunities to meet other exchange student and explore the country.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The beginning of my exchange was a bit confusing. For me, I really like being able to plan ahead, and coming to a new country I wanted to know everything about how my semester was going to be like. But we didn't get all the information (like schedule and proffessors, what to do and where to go) right when arriving, as things were still being figured out. So we had to wait a bit for all of that.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: When I arrived, I was called in for a "registration day" at the Erasmus office at the university, where I was shortly introduced to the Erasmus coordinator. The week after that she held a "welcome day" on zoom where she answered a lot of our questions about the semester. The Erasmus coordinator was also very nice at helping through mail if there was any questions during the semester.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: For me it was pretty easy to find housing as I started to look for accomodation pretty long in advance. I found housing through the website StayInAthens, that had accomodation for Erasmus students. Though a lot of people also found housing on social media. I would recommend using the Instagram page ELA housing to find accomodation.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Its a bit difficult to figure out which neighboorhoods are nice to live in before arriving at the destination, if you, like me, have never been there before. It is worth considering how close to the center you want to live, and how close to campus you want to be. In Athens I would recommend living close to a metro station, as it is definitly the quickest and most reliable form of public transportation. I also enjoyed not living directly in the center, as the neigborhoods a bit outside of the center are a lot more calm than in the center, while stille only being a short metro ride away. If you go to Panteion University, I would recommend searching for accomodation in Koukaki, Neos Kosmos or Kallithea, as these areas are close to the center, uni and the beach.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The quality of the apartments available for students weren't the best in my experience. I ended up liking my area quite a lot, but i wasn't that sattisfied with the maintenance of the apartment.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: In Greece everything is done over mail, which takes some patience.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: When arriving in Athens, a registration day is scheduled, where you basically go to the Erasmus office to sign some contract. Then after the Erasmus coordinator has a welcome day, the schedule of the courses available for Erasmus students are send out. (It is also possible to follow courses in greek, but in these you don't go to the classes, but plan an individual study program with the professor from the course). When you have the schedule you can start attending classes to figure out which ones you want to register for. You then have to register for them on the uniersity's online platform where you can write with the professors and see the assignments for the class. After some time you have to oficially register for the course, by sending a registration form to the erasmus office, which they sign.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Erasmus coordinator and the professors helps you through the process, though its your own responsibility to manage which classes to take/which requirements there are for the courses etc.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I managed to register for the courses I wanted. As I chose only courses from Social Anthropology which was the department I was registered in, I was "first in line" in the courses where there was a limited space.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't stress about it too much. Even though it's done in a different pace than back home, most people manage to get the courses they want. And just ask your professors or the Erasmus office if you have questions, they are there to help, and they all know that its overwhelming to be an exchange student.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really liked the quality of the academic programme. Though there wasn't that many courses within anthropology to choose from, and it was a bit difficult to take courses from the other departments in the university, as the ECTS points of the courses were different in the different departments.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was about the same as back home I believe. The professors expected you to have some prior knowledge to the subjects, though people in class were from different study programs, so we had different skills.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching were very different from back home. In 3/4 of my classes we were only 8-10 students in a class. And we all sat around a table and discussed the lectures with the professor. So is was very engaging and you had to participate a lot compared to a lecture back home. The exams were pretty much the same as back home, same lenght and difficulty, though one of my exams had to be written in class by hand, which was a bit different.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
History of the Balkan people
Ethnography of non-western states
Digital anthropology
Anthropology and critical discourse studies

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I was really surprised about the ethnography of non-western states course, as the professor Makris was very engaging and the subject were very interesting. I also really enjoyed the digital anthropology course.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
When I first arrived I just wanted to have my public transportation handled for the rest of the semester, so i bought an
Ath.ena
card for 6 months (which was very cheap for students). But i didn't consider that I would be going to the airport a lot to pick up guests from home, so I didn't include this in my card, which meant I had to pay extra every time I wanted to go to the airport. I would recommend just buying the
Ath.ena
card for one month at a time, so that you can include the airport in the months where you know you will use that.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Public transport was very cheap! Food was maybe a bit more expensive, especially in the touristy areas.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The non-academic oppotunities very very good in Athens, if you know where to find them. There are a lot of groups on social media (especially instagram) where you can find friends and things to do. I would recommend following ELA (Erasmus Life Athens) that has trips, parties, yoga, and other events for international people, and the ESN departments. Its important to know that you can go to events/on trips with the different ESN departments, and not just the ESN department for your own university, so make sure to follow the different departments on social media, so you don't miss out on opportunities.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are a lot of opportunities. There are gyms, sports days, greek language course, trips within Athens and outside of Athens, events like speed friending, beer pong, parties and the list goes on. I believe that you can fill almost every day with non-academic activities if you wanted.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would definitly recommend going on the weekend trips arranged by ESN and ELA. Almost every sunday there is one or more trip you can go on, and sometimes there are longer trips. I think this is a great way to meet new people, and to explore the country.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Again I would recommend using the opportunites that ELA and ESN provide, especially in the beginning where you also want to make new friends. I would definitely see both the main land as well as the islands, as Greece has so much different things and places to experience.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: People were very welcoming and friendly. The language is very difficult, but most people a pretty good at speaking english.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I didn't socialize that much with the local students, mostly with other international students, but i would recommend talking to the people who arrange the trips and events for Erasmus students, as they are mostly local students, but are very open and easy to talk to.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The mentality is very different and more relaxed than in Denmark, so that takes a bit of time getting used to, but its definitly something you get used to, and end up admiring!

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The kindness of the people. Everyone I met was very open and friendly.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Make sure to go on a lot of trips and try to experience as much of Greece as possible, you will not regret it!
Make an effort in the beginning to meet people, go to events and on trips with other exchange students, even though you might not have anyone to go there with. You will definitly meet a lot of nice people there you can talk to!
Find your local farmers market! Here you can get a lot of fresh and delicious greens and veggies to a much cheaper price than in the super market.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just definitly use all the opportunities you are given as an exchange student, do some research beforehand about things you want to experience in and around Athens and don't wait until the end to do them all.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Makingfriends with people from different cultural backgrounds than yourself.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Learning to be more spontanious and managing to navigate in a pretty unorganized country as a Dane who plans everything ahead.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
